hook: I'm rebuilding every piece of a modern LLM by hand, and nothing counts until it matches PyTorch to the last decimal.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — I'm rebuilding every piece of a modern LLM by hand, and nothing counts until it matches PyTorch to the last decimal.

0:15 QUESTION — Using GPT or Claude is easy. Explaining why Llama 3 uses RMSNorm, or why FlashAttention is exact and still faster, is what frontier lab interviews actually test. I'm an EE and Army veteran, and the only way I trust my understanding is to build it and check it.

1:00 INTUITION — Show the map: 18 modules, 216 episodes, from tensors to an inference engine that serves Qwen3. Mac for the first 5 modules, rented GPUs after that. [EXPLAINER plays here: the curriculum as a subway map, with nine flagship projects as the stations.]

2:45 MATH — One equation, because it is the whole series in miniature. softmax(x)_i = exp(x_i) / sum_j exp(x_j). Then the identity softmax(x) = softmax(x - c) for any constant c, because exp(-c) cancels top and bottom. Remember this. It comes back in the FlashAttention module.

4:00 CODE — Repo tour on screen: curriculum/curriculum.json (every episode, its build, its sources), code/<module>/eNN_*.py (one runnable file per episode, tests at the bottom), prep/ (my notes), explainers/ (the Manim scenes). Run print_map() and read the 18 modules out loud with their hardware.

6:00 CODE — The receipt rule, live. Type softmax_naive(x, dim=-1): e = torch.exp(x); return e / e.sum(dim, keepdim=True). Type receipt(mine, ref, name) that wraps torch.testing.assert_close and prints PASS or FAIL. Test on randn(4, 8) logits: PASS. It looks done.

7:30 RECEIPT — Multiply the logits by 100 and run the same receipt. FAIL, because exp(800) is inf in float32 and inf / inf is nan. Add softmax_stable: subtract x.amax(dim, keepdim=True) first. Receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(softmax_stable(big), torch.softmax(big, -1)) passes at scales 1, 100 and 1e4.
9:00 MEASURE — Show torch.isnan(softmax_naive(big)).any() is True, and the largest safe float32 input to exp is about 88.7. A test that only uses small inputs would have shipped this bug.

10:00 TAKEAWAY — Every from-scratch piece in this series ends with a check against the production implementation. Interview line: I don't say I understand attention, I say my implementation matches SDPA within float32 tolerance, and here is the test.

10:45 NEXT — The projects: FlashAttention in Triton, an inference engine, a 4D parallel trainer, a reasoning RL reproduction. All built on this habit. Next: Setup: uv, PyTorch, MPS vs CUDA, RunPod in 10 minutes.
key_math: softmax(x)_i = exp(x_i) / sum_j exp(x_j); softmax(x - c) = softmax(x) for any scalar c; stable form uses c = max_j x_j so the largest exponent is exp(0) = 1.
code_task: print_map() reads curriculum/curriculum.json and prints each module code, episode count, name, hardware, and the 216 total. softmax_naive(x, dim=-1) and softmax_stable(x, dim=-1) on x of shape (4, 8). receipt(mine, ref, name) wraps torch.testing.assert_close and prints PASS/FAIL.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(softmax_stable(x * s), torch.softmax(x * s, -1)) for s in (1, 100, 1e4) passes; softmax_naive(x * 100) fails with nan; pytest asserts 18 modules and 216 episodes.
gotchas: assert_close default tolerances depend on dtype (float32 is rtol 1.3e-6, atol 1e-5), so compare in the same dtype; forgetting keepdim=True in the sum broadcasts (4,) against (4, 8) and errors or silently divides the wrong axis; testing only on small random inputs hides overflow bugs.
interview_q: How do you know your reimplementation is correct? I test it against the reference implementation on adversarial inputs, large magnitudes, odd shapes, low precision, using assert_close with dtype-appropriate tolerances, and I gradcheck the backward in float64.
explainer: Here is the whole series as one map, eighteen modules running from a single tensor to a serving engine for a real model.
The first five stops run on a Mac. After the transformer module, the line switches to rented GPUs by the hour.
Along the line sit nine flagship projects. Each one is unlocked by the modules right before it, like FlashAttention after the GPU module.
Every station has the same rule. We build the piece from scratch, then we compare it to PyTorch's own version, number by number.
Here is the rule catching a real bug. Our naive softmax matches PyTorch on small logits, so the check turns green.
Scale the logits by one hundred and the exponential overflows to infinity. Infinity over infinity is not a number, and the check turns red.
Subtract the max first and the biggest exponent becomes one. Same answer, no overflow, and the receipt passes at every scale.

short: The 7:30 RECEIPT beat: naive softmax passes, multiply by 100, it returns nan, one line fixes it. Caption: 'This softmax passes every test. Until it doesn't.'
yt_title: LLMs from First Principles: build every piece, check it vs PyTorch

hook: Same script, my laptop GPU and a rented RTX 4090. The gap is bigger than you think, and we measure it exactly.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Same script, my laptop GPU and a rented RTX 4090. The gap is bigger than you think, and we measure it exactly.

0:15 QUESTION — Half of ML bugs are environment bugs: the wrong torch build, a GPU you are not actually using, a timer that measures nothing. Before we touch a tensor we need one environment that works the same on an M4 Mac and on a CUDA box, and a way to rent an H100 without waking up to a surprise bill.

1:00 INTUITION — The GPU is a separate machine you send work to. Calls return before the work is done. [EXPLAINER plays here: CPU queues kernels, GPU drains them, the timer only means something after a sync.]

2:30 MATH — Matmul cost: C = A B with A (n, n) and B (n, n) has n^2 outputs, each needing n multiplies and n adds, so FLOPs = 2 n^3. At n = 4096 that is 1.37e11 FLOPs. TFLOP/s = 2 n^3 / seconds / 1e12. This one formula is how we will judge every kernel in the series.

3:30 CODE — Terminal: uv init, uv add torch pytest, uv run python -c 'import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.backends.mps.is_available())'. Commit uv.lock so the RunPod box gets the same versions.

4:30 CODE — env_check.py: pick_device() prefers cuda, then mps, then cpu. sync(device) calls torch.cuda.synchronize() or torch.mps.synchronize(). dtype_works(dtype, device) tries an 8x8 matmul inside try/except. matmul_tflops(n, dtype, device, iters=20): randn A and B, 3 warmup matmuls, sync, time 20 matmuls, sync, return 2 n^3 / secs / 1e12.

7:00 CODE — RunPod in 3 minutes: put a small prepaid credit on the account so the balance is the hard spend cap, launch a 1x RTX 4090 pod with a PyTorch template, git clone, uv sync, uv run env_check.py. Stop the pod from the console the moment the run ends, and say out loud what an idle pod costs per hour.

8:30 RECEIPT — Speed means nothing if the answer is wrong. test_matmul_is_correct_on_device: compute a @ b in float64 on CPU as the reference, the same matmul in float32 on the device, and torch.testing.assert_close(got.double(), ref, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-3). Passes on MPS and CUDA. Also show float64 fails on MPS in dtype_works.

9:30 MEASURE — The table: float32, bfloat16, float16 TFLOP/s at n = 4096 on M4 MPS, M4 CPU, and RTX 4090. Compare each to the vendor's quoted peak and say the percentage. Then remove the sync calls and rerun: the numbers become absurd, which proves the timer was lying.

11:00 TAKEAWAY — One lockfile, one env_check, and every benchmark synchronizes before it stops the clock. Interview line: GPU work is asynchronous, so a benchmark without a device sync measures launch overhead, not compute.
11:30 NEXT — This env_check and spend-cap habit is what lets us run the 8xH100 pretraining speedrun project later for the price of lunch. Next: Tensors: what they actually are.
key_math: FLOPs(matmul n x n x n) = 2 n^3; TFLOP/s = 2 n^3 / t / 1e12; percent of peak = measured / vendor peak.
code_task: env_check.py with pick_device() -> torch.device, sync(device), dtype_works(dtype, device) -> bool via an (8, 8) matmul, matmul_tflops(n=4096, dtype, device, iters=20) -> float, report() printing python/torch versions, device name, and a dtype x TFLOP/s table for float32, bfloat16, float16 plus a CPU float32 baseline at n=2048.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close((a.float().to(dev) @ b.float().to(dev)).cpu().double(), a @ b, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-3) with a, b float64 (256, 256) on CPU; assert dtype_works(torch.bfloat16, 'mps') on macOS 14+.
gotchas: Timing without torch.mps.synchronize()/torch.cuda.synchronize() gives impossible TFLOP/s; float64 is not supported on MPS, so code that calls .double() on device crashes; on CUDA, float32 matmul uses full FP32 unless you call torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('high') to allow TF32, which changes your benchmark by several x; an idle RunPod pod keeps billing until it is stopped.
interview_q: Your benchmark says your kernel hits 2000 TFLOP/s on an H100. What went wrong? Almost certainly a missing device synchronize, so the timer measured how fast Python queued launches. Warm up, sync before and after, average many iterations, and sanity check against the hardware peak.
explainer: On the left is the CPU running our Python. On the right is the GPU, a separate machine with its own memory and its own queue.
When we call a matmul, the CPU drops a kernel into the GPU's queue and returns immediately, before any multiplying has happened.
If we stop the timer now, we have measured how fast Python can drop boxes into a queue. The GPU has not started.
A synchronize call makes the CPU wait at the door until the queue is empty. Only now does the timer measure real compute.
The work itself is easy to count. Every one of the n squared outputs needs n multiplies and n adds, so two n cubed operations.
Divide that count by the synced time and we get TFLOP slash s, one honest number we can compare against the chip's spec sheet.
explainer_visuals: Two boxes: 'CPU / Python' left, 'GPU' right, with a horizontal queue (conveyor belt) between them.
A 'matmul' block slides onto the conveyor; the Python cursor immediately moves to the next line.
A stopwatch freezes at 0.01 ms while the block is still sitting at the start of the conveyor, a red question mark.
A 'sync' gate closes on the CPU side; blocks drain through the GPU; stopwatch resumes and stops when the belt is empty.
An n x n output grid, one cell highlighted, its row of A and column of B lighting up with n multiply and n add ticks; formula 2n^3 appears.
A bar chart: measured TFLOP/s for M4 MPS, CPU, RTX 4090 beside dashed vendor peak lines.
short: The 9:30 MEASURE beat: run the benchmark with and without synchronize, watch the fake number appear. Caption: 'Your GPU benchmark is probably lying to you.'
yt_title: PyTorch setup with uv: MPS vs CUDA vs RunPod, and honest TFLOPs
x_post: GPU calls are async. Time a matmul without torch.mps.synchronize() and you measure Python queueing, not compute. Built one env_check.py that runs on an M4 Mac and a rented 4090, with real TFLOP/s for fp32/bf16/fp16. Code + video:
linkedin: Set up a reproducible PyTorch environment with uv that runs unchanged on an M4 Mac (MPS) and a rented RTX 4090. I wrote an env check that measures matmul TFLOP/s per dtype and verifies the device result against a float64 CPU reference. The lesson: without a device synchronize, a benchmark reports numbers the hardware physically cannot reach.
